title: Transferable safety constraints built into socio-technical systems

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a reusable engineering method that connects hazard analysis to implemented safety constraints and continuing evidence that those constraints work. It would help designers specify the conditions and behaviors needed to prevent or contain defined hazards, incorporate those constraints into equipment, software, human responsibilities and organizational controls, and maintain their effectiveness throughout operation. Transferability would require independent teams to obtain convincing results across substantially different systems using a common method.

Its technical foundation is a system-level view of safety. Dangerous outcomes can arise through interactions among functioning components, people, software and organizations. System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) examines control structures, unsafe control actions and scenarios that can produce losses. Its outputs can inform functional requirements, architecture and test plans. The proposed capability extends this pathway through demonstrably effective implementation and sustained operational assurance.

Every assurance would have a defined scope, including the losses and hazards considered, system boundaries, operating conditions and assumptions about people, equipment and the environment. Changes in those conditions would require reassessment. The concept belongs to industrial engineering through socio-technical system design and lifecycle safety, with contributions from systems engineering, control engineering, human factors, reliability engineering and software verification.

significance.text: A transferable method could make architectural protection more systematic across industrial and service systems. Designers could use identified hazardous interactions to shape control authority, feedback, requirements and testing early in development. STPA already describes this architectural role. The prospective advance is reliable execution of that role across settings, accompanied by evidence that the resulting constraints remain effective.

Conditional impact assessment. If the method substantially reduced serious hazards across different settings, it could shift more protection into system architecture and reduce dependence on training and after-the-fact detection. Reusable assurance practices could also help teams assess the safety implications of equipment replacement, software updates and organizational changes. These downstream benefits would depend on the quality of implementation, the coverage of the analysis and the resources available to maintain the controls.

Comparison with major historical changes in industrial safety practice is an evaluative analogy whose force would depend on demonstrated risk reduction and broad adoption. Claims of effectiveness would remain bounded by specified hazards, operating envelopes and assumptions. Unknown hazards, incomplete models, degradation and changing organizational conditions would continue to create residual risk.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is a transferable, verifiable transition from interaction-based hazard analysis to enforceable and maintainable safety constraints. Analysts must turn unsafe control actions and loss scenarios into precise requirements, allocate those requirements to the people and technical elements capable of enforcing them, and show that the implemented system satisfies them. The NASA aircraft study gives a concrete example of this translation difficulty. Its authors reported that the STPA Handbook did not directly guide their transition from analysis results to finalized requirements, and their work left the constraint set incomplete. This is evidence from one team's experience, influenced in part by resource limitations.

Analysis boundaries and traceability are substantial engineering barriers. A team must include interactions that materially affect safety, connect unsafe control actions to higher-level hazards, and preserve those links through requirements and verification. The NASA application reported additional risks when boundaries expanded, while omitting explicit links from unsafe control actions to higher-level hazards. Its limited independent comparison also left questions about the additional value of the analysis unresolved. Prioritization and verification require further work, and the authors found insufficient evidence that STPA could fully replace the approaches serving those functions in their application.

Continuing assurance must account for change. Control algorithms can become inadequate as system conditions change, and sensors and actuators can degrade. Human responsibilities, organizational practices and operating environments can also evolve. A practical method must identify when its assumptions have weakened and support reassessment of the affected constraints. The supplied sources establish mechanisms that motivate this requirement, while leaving the difficulty and effectiveness of a general operational solution unquantified.

Engineering synthesis. Transferability adds a further challenge because different domains have different hazards, control structures, evidence and operational constraints. A common method would need to preserve enough specificity to produce enforceable requirements while remaining reproducible across those differences. Demonstrating its practical value would also require credible comparisons with existing safety engineering and explicit accounting for analysis effort, implementation burden and maintenance costs.

current_state.text: Nancy G. Leveson and John P. Thomas's March 2018 STPA Handbook documents a structured process for defining losses, hazards and system-level constraints, modeling control structures, identifying unsafe control actions and developing loss scenarios. It connects analysis outputs to requirements, architecture and testing. The supplied review examined a truncated extraction covering pages 1–50. Although the earlier research cited Chapter 3 around page 59, inspected earlier pages independently support these methodological claims.

The supplied research identifies the FAA report Evaluation of System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) for Improving Aviation Safety, attributed to John P. Thomas and John G. Van Houdt, as DOT/FAA/TC-24/16, dated 1 July 2024. The research says its repository description discussed aviation applications, benefits, limitations and hands-on work. The source index retains no artifact for this citation, and the validated review had no source text with which to verify that account or assess the report's findings. Its substantive conclusions therefore remain unverified within the supplied evidence.

A 2026 NASA study by Matthew P. Huffman, James M. Green and Tinicia J. Menifee applied STPA to an early hybrid-electric aircraft concept, focusing on its energy storage system and electric powertrain. The repository lists a meeting on August 17–20, 2026. The team reported that expanding the analysis boundaries could expose additional risks and suggested that rigorous traditional methods using broader boundaries might obtain similar results. That suggestion requires qualification because the independent hazard-analysis comparison was limited.

The NASA application remained preliminary. It left the full constraint set undeveloped, omitted explicit links between unsafe control actions and higher-level hazards, and completed only a limited independent comparison. Its authors identified unresolved prioritization and verification needs. These details constrain what the study establishes about completed safety requirements, comparative performance and operational effectiveness. The validated review used prose spanning all 19 pages of the paper, with no declared text truncation. Figure images were uninspected, so figure-dependent interpretations remain outside that assessment.

Evidence-scope synthesis. The supplied materials establish an existing analysis method and an early aircraft application. Cross-system transferability, sustained operational assurance and substantial realized risk reduction remain to be demonstrated in this record. No bounded freshness search was supplied, so the materials cannot establish the field-wide state as of 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Independent teams would apply a common design and assurance method to several substantially different high-consequence systems. Before deployment, each team would specify the losses, hazards, system boundaries, operating envelope, assumptions and measurable safety constraints. The demonstration plan would define what counts as a substantially different system and justify the selected range of applications. These are proposed evidentiary requirements.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams apply a common method across substantially different high-consequence systems

completion_criteria.text: Proposed implementation evidence. Each application would preserve traceability from hazards through unsafe control actions and loss scenarios to finalized requirements, implemented controls and verification results. Independent review and fault injection or other realistic testing would examine whether the constraints prevent or contain specified hazardous scenarios, including foreseeable human and equipment failures. Testing would address relevant timing, feedback, degradation and operating-context assumptions. This proposal responds to the documented transition and verification gaps.
completion_criteria.label: Hazard-traceable implemented constraints prevent or contain specified hazardous scenarios

completion_criteria.text: Proposed effectiveness evidence. Prospective operating observations and comparison with credible existing safety engineering would assess risk reduction and continued constraint effectiveness. Before execution, teams would define the sampling approach, safety metrics, observation periods, uncertainty treatment and the improvement needed to justify a claim of substantial benefit. Reports would disclose residual risk, missed hazards, constraint violations, implementation effort and maintenance costs. The supplied sources provide no established numerical thresholds for these proposals.
completion_criteria.label: Prospective comparisons assess risk reduction and continued constraint effectiveness

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries. Independent teams would need sufficient access to the method, assumptions, analysis records and verification procedures to reproduce the reasoning and evaluate the results. Demonstrations would examine how assurance is maintained when equipment, software, organizational responsibilities or operating conditions change. Finite applications and tests would establish demonstrated breadth within their stated conditions. Any broader claim would require additional evidence, with the boundaries of each assurance made explicit.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce assurance reasoning within explicit demonstrated boundaries

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. IND-01, General-purpose, rapidly reconfigurable production, overlaps through the safety implications of changing production configurations. Transferable safety constraints could help govern permitted reconfigurations and reassessment after change. IND-01 concerns production flexibility, while IND-06 concerns safety constraint design and assurance across socio-technical systems.

Roster-based synthesis. IND-02, Production-time qualification of individual critical parts, could provide evidence relevant to equipment assumptions and component-related hazards. Its focus is the qualification of individual parts. IND-06 addresses system-level interactions, including control, software, human and organizational contributions to safety.

Roster-based synthesis. IND-03, A predictive and testable science of supply-network cascade containment, shares an interest in interacting systems and the containment of harmful propagation. Supply-network predictions could inform hazards and constraints in a networked operation. IND-03 centers on supply-network cascades, while IND-06 centers on transferable safety engineering and lifecycle assurance.

Roster-based synthesis. IND-04, Economical mixed-product disassembly and recovery, offers a potential application setting in which changing products, equipment and worker interactions would require safety controls. Its central objective is economical recovery. IND-06 would address the definition, implementation and maintenance of safety constraints within such operations.

Roster-based synthesis. IND-05, Transferable prediction and prevention of work-related human performance risk, has close overlap through human actions, working conditions and organizational influences. Its predictions and interventions could inform safety requirements. IND-06 spans the wider control structure connecting people, software, equipment and organizations, including hazardous interactions involving functioning components.

The NASA paper's figure images were uninspected, leaving figure-dependent details unassessed.

brief.title: Reusable ways to build safety into complex systems
possible: Designers could use a shared method to turn identified dangers into safety rules built into machines, software and people's responsibilities. They could test whether those rules prevent or contain harm and keep working as equipment and organisations change.
why: For people working in or relying on industrial and service systems, more protection could be built into how those systems operate. Safety would depend less on training and spotting problems after they arise.
Teams could also use the same approach to assess how software updates, equipment replacements and changes in responsibility affect safety.

sources.who: Nancy G. Leveson and John P. Thomas
sources.showed: Their handbook describes STPA, a method for finding hazards in interactions among people, equipment and software. It connects this analysis to design requirements and testing, and reports comparisons that found lower analysis costs.
sources.quote:
In addition, STPA turned out to be much less costly in terms of time and resources than the 
traditional methods.
sources.cited_for: It provides the analysis method that could guide safety rules built into a system's design.
sources.not_established: It does not establish a reusable path to implemented protections that remain effective across different systems.

sources.who: John P. Thomas and John G. Van Houdt

sources.cited_for: It concerns evaluation of the method for aviation safety.
sources.not_established: An aviation evaluation alone would not establish effectiveness across substantially different systems.

sources.who: Matthew P. Huffman, James M. Green and Tinicia J. Menifee
sources.showed: The team applied the method to an early aircraft concept's batteries and electric propulsion. Expanding the analysis boundaries revealed additional risks, but the team left the full safety requirements unfinished.
sources.quote:
Findings show STPA provides a structured, comprehensive hazard evaluation and can identify 
additional risks by expanding analysis boundaries.
sources.cited_for: The study demonstrates an early application and the difficulty of turning analysis into completed safety requirements.
sources.not_established: This preliminary application did not demonstrate working protections, sustained risk reduction or superiority to existing methods.

shown: Nancy Leveson and John Thomas have described a structured way to find dangerous interactions and use them to guide design and testing. This addresses hazards that can arise even when individual components work as intended.

A NASA-led team applied the method to an early aircraft concept and found additional risks by widening its analysis. The work remained preliminary: safety requirements were incomplete, and comparison with existing methods was limited.
missing: A demonstrated path from identified hazards to precise safety rules, assigned responsibilities and working protections is still needed.
Independent teams have yet to demonstrate that a common method works across substantially different systems.
Continued protection through equipment wear, software updates and organisational change remains to be demonstrated.
Credible operating comparisons must establish substantial risk reduction alongside implementation and maintenance costs.

milestones.label: Independent teams apply a shared method across different systems
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to apply a common method across substantially different systems where failure could cause serious harm, defining hazards, conditions and measurable safety rules. This would test transferability.

milestones.label: Implemented protections prevent or contain specified hazards
milestones.explanation: Each application would have to link hazards to implemented protections and pass independent review and realistic failure tests. This would show that the analysis produces working safeguards.

milestones.label: Operating comparisons show lasting risk reduction
milestones.explanation: Planned operating comparisons would have to show lasting risk reduction against credible existing practice, using agreed measures and reporting remaining risks and costs. This would establish practical benefit.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce the safety reasoning within clear limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce the safety reasoning and assess protection through changes in equipment, software, responsibilities and operating conditions. This would establish where the method remains dependable.

uncertain: How different must the tested systems be before the method counts as transferable?
What size and duration of improvement would establish substantial benefit at an acceptable cost?
How much additional value does this method provide over existing safety analysis applied with equally broad boundaries?

page.title: Safety-driven design of socio-technical systems
page.definition: People, software and equipment can each act as intended and still cause harm through their interaction. System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA) identifies how that could happen and derives safety constraints: conditions the system must maintain or actions it must require or prevent. Those constraints guide equipment design, software behaviour and organisational responsibilities. Independent teams in different industries demonstrate that the safeguards work in operation and after changes.

goal.need: Three passengers died in the crash of Asiana flight 214. Its low-airspeed alert was designed for cruise. On approach, the height above ground and the time the engines and pilots need to respond also matter. A warning that accounts for all three could give pilots time to recover. Making an alert more reliable cannot correct a warning that arrives too late. Some hazards emerge only in service, so crews and operators need evidence that safeguards work under the conditions in which they use them.

completion.title: Independent teams reproduce verified safety-driven design through operation in different industries.
completion.criterion: Independently led applications in different industries use the same method to derive hazard-linked safety constraints, implement and validate all selected controls, obtain acceptance of residual risk, and meet approved operational monitoring targets for their specified durations. After safety-relevant changes, affected controls are revalidated and new or increased risks accepted. Achievement is limited to the hazards, operating conditions and applications demonstrated.
completion.set_by: Technology Atlas; proposed cross-industry operational replication test.
completion.basis: Searched the STPA Handbook, SAE J3307/J3187 public scopes, FAA evaluation and guidance, and MIL-STD-882E for a cross-industry operational replication criterion. None was found, including a required replication count, common risk-reduction margin or observation duration. This proposed test combines their analysis, verification and lifecycle objectives; the cited evaluations do not establish its completion.

milestones.title: STPA on a pilot system yields controller constraints linked to hazards and loss scenarios.
milestones.criterion: Identify losses and system hazards, then model who or what issues each control action and what feedback it receives. Examine whether an action could cause a hazard through omission, through provision, through incorrect timing or order, or through incorrect duration where duration applies. Link unsafe actions to hazards, derive the corresponding controller constraints, and identify scenarios in which unsafe actions occur or safe actions fail to take effect.
milestones.set_by: STPA practitioner method documented by Leveson and Thomas, STPA Handbook, Chapter 2; recognised in FAA guidance, Appendix C.2.37.
milestones.threshold_quote: each UCA can be inverted to define constraints for each controller.

milestones.title: A system implements all selected risk controls and validates their effectiveness.
milestones.criterion: Verify that every selected mitigation has been implemented and validate its effectiveness by appropriate analysis, testing, demonstration or inspection. Record the verification and validation in the hazard tracking system. Check safety-significant hardware, software and procedures against the applicable safety requirements.
milestones.set_by: US Department of Defense system-safety programme; MIL-STD-882E, Change 1, §4.3.6 and Task 401, for DoD systems.
milestones.threshold_quote: Document the verification and validation in the HTS.

milestones.title: The authority accepts risk before a known hazard exposes people, equipment or the environment.
milestones.criterion: Before exposing people, equipment or the environment to a known system hazard, obtain risk acceptance from the designated authority. For a Serious or High risk, obtain formal concurrence from the user representative before the acceptance decision.
milestones.set_by: US Department of Defense system-safety programme; MIL-STD-882E, Change 1, §4.3.7, for DoD systems.
milestones.threshold_quote: Before exposing people, equipment, or the environment to known system-related hazards, the risks shall be accepted

milestones.title: An operating system meets its safety performance targets for the approved monitoring duration.
milestones.criterion: For a hazard with an approved monitoring plan, start the reporting period once all required mitigations have been implemented. Complete monitoring for the full duration specified in the plan and meet its measurable safety performance targets. At that point the FAA treats the predicted residual risk as verified.
milestones.set_by: Federal Aviation Administration, FAA Safety Risk Management Guidance, §§3.8.3 and 5.3; criterion published for FAA safety issues.
milestones.threshold_quote: monitoring activities have been completed through the reporting duration and safety performance targets have been met

milestones.title: After a fielded system changes, affected controls are revalidated and revised risks accepted.
milestones.criterion: A fielded system's changed interfaces, users, hardware, software or missions undergo hazard and risk reassessment. Resulting mitigations are verified and validated; the responsible authority accepts risks from new hazards and increased risks from known hazards.
milestones.set_by: US Department of Defense system-safety programme; MIL-STD-882E, Change 1, §§4.3 and 4.3.8, for DoD systems.
milestones.threshold_quote: revised risk will need to be formally accepted

milestones.title: The design traces each identified hazard through its causal scenarios to the features that prevent them.
milestones.criterion: For each identified hazard, the design record links its causal scenarios to the features chosen to prevent them. A reviewer can follow a link from a feature back to the scenario and hazard that explain why the feature is needed.
milestones.set_by: Nancy Leveson and John Thomas, STPA Handbook, chapters 3 and 7.
milestones.threshold_quote: STPA incorporates complete traceability from identified hazards to their causal scenarios and to the design features that are used to prevent them.

not_found: The full normative texts of SAE J3307 and J3187 were not accessible; their public scopes were available.

results.finding: One illustrative aircraft wheel-braking system yielded six hazard-linked autobrake constraints.
results.detail: The example leaves some timing, speed, and braking thresholds to be determined.

results.finding: NASA's STPA pilot on one SUSAN Electrofan concept evaluated approximately 180 unsafe control actions.
results.detail: The examples cover ground charging and battery ventilation. Duration was inapplicable to those discrete commands. Appendix B documents scenarios in which the emergency battery command is omitted or fails to take effect.
results.quote:
Evaluating approximately 180 UCAs across roughly ten loss -scenario 
categories results in a very large analysis matrix.

results.finding: STPA of one clinician–AI diagnostic prototype identified 22 loss scenarios.
results.detail: The analysis covers clinician–CADx interaction. Data quality, algorithmic failure analysis and image acquisition were outside its stated scope.
results.quote: There are a total of 22 loss scenarios identified through this process, capturing a wide range of potential failures in clinician-AI interaction.

results.finding: One CADx prototype traces interface features through 6 safety design guidelines.
results.detail: Table 3 omits UCA-1, failure to provide a preliminary diagnosis. Its two scenarios include a software malfunction and failure by the clinician to start the system.
results.quote:
Table
3
summarizes the traceability between identified UCAs, the derived safety design guidelines, and their implementation in the proposed GUI.

results.finding: Across 40 dermoscopic test images, gradient-based explanations had a mean intersection over union of 0.13.
results.detail: The study measured explanation overlap. Effects on clinician interpretation, trust and workload await clinician studies.
results.quote: The mean IoU across the test set was 0.13, indicating low spatial consistency between gradient-based methods.

results.finding: Caribbean RVSM in 2025 (57 validated large height deviations) had an estimated overall vertical collision risk of 3.957 × 10⁻⁹ fatal accidents per flight hour.
results.quote:
The sum of this 
value and the technical risk estimate for airspace is 3.957 × 10-9 fapfh, which meets the overall safety goal 
of 5.0 × 10-9 fapfh.

results.detail: Risk acceptance is evidenced by the FAA’s approval and conditional lifting of the grounding. Operators had to complete the mandated modifications, maintenance actions, and pilot training before resuming operations.
